Serializable only promises that some total order over transactions exists and is legal.
Nothing in that promise says the order has to agree with when things actually happened.

lines: Watch what the checker is actually required to satisfy here, and what it isn't.
Every transaction, as a whole, gets placed somewhere in one shared order, and each one's reads have to make sense given what came before it in that order.
That's the entire requirement. Feed it the hook's own history and an order exists: put the refresh first.
Notice that nothing about the database itself changed between this check and the last one.
One extra rule got added: if a transaction finished before another one began, the order has to agree with that.
Run the exact same search under that one extra rule, and this time nothing comes back. Not a different answer. No answer.
Pay attention to which half of this was measured and which half is just a documented promise.
A transaction that opens after a commit finishes saw it, every time, because of how snapshots get taken, not because of any promise written down anywhere.
A transaction already running when a sibling committed never saw that commit, even on its very next read, taken well after the commit was done.

Separate what actually forces an order here from what merely could have.
These two transactions never touched the same data, so nothing requires one to come before the other in real time or in the serial order.
A database is free to reverse them, and that freedom has nothing to do with a stale read or a bug.
Carry forward the shape of the whole relationship, not just two words that rhyme.
Serializable: one order over whole transactions, nothing about when. Strict serializable: the identical check, with the clock added back in.
One of those was measured directly on a real database today, not taken on faith from a name.
Before you answer, think about what freedom concurrency normally buys a database, and what happens when there's none of it.
With zero concurrency, there was never a second legal order to choose between in the first place.
answer: Yes, and the reason is almost too simple to notice.
Run every transaction fully, one at a time, in submission order, and that order is the only legal one there is.
Since each transaction finishes before the next starts, that same order already respects real time. The extra rule costs nothing when there was never a choice to begin with.
